english: The expression "all objects" refers to each and every object from basic physical matter on up to the omniscience of a Buddha. They all exist in dependence upon their parts, so in a manner of speaking their "cause and effect can never fail." The antithesis, which we seek to disprove, is that these objects could have the solid existence they appear to have: that they could exist naturally. "When they lose all solid appearance"--that is, when we perceive that there is not a single thing in the universe which has any true or natural existence--then we have found "the path that pleases the Buddhas."

english: One might have the following thought: "These mental afflictions are empty of any natural kind of existence, but at the same time they do appear to have natural existence, and so they are like an illusion. As long as this is the case--because they do exist through some nature of their own--I could never eliminate them from their root." It is good though if I can eliminate this fear from my heart, and rely on the practice of making great efforts to remove my mental afflictions, through working to develop the wisdom which perceives emptiness. Given that I therefore have at the present moment the ability to remove these afflictions, it is not good on the other hand that I subject myself pointlessly to the sufferings of the lower realms, to hells and the rest. Why should I put myself through these pains? Some commentators have also explained the previous lines as referring to the fact that, once we remove the seeds for the mental afflictions, they can no longer stay in these various places.

english: And if you say it is possible, then let us ask you a question. english: To summarize, we must undertake to meditate upon the real nature of things, basing this analysis upon the practice of meditative quietude. The "me" you think of when you say "it's mine" is nothing more than a projection that you lay on the heaps or parts that make you up. It has not the slightest bit of any natural existence, of any definitive existence, of any independent way of being. The existence of a person is something which happens only by virtue of an idea; the person exists only through projections, only in dependence on other things, and nothing more. Practice thinking of things this way: see that they have no nature of their own. Continue in your meditation, applying this same concept to every existing object: to the parts of a person, and everything else as well. Contemplation Thirty-Seven Pray They All Be Bodhisattvas (The following contemplations are all from the "Chapter on Dedication")

english: One might have the following thought: "These mental afflictions are empty of any natural kind of existence, but at the same time they do appear to have natural existence, and so they are like an illusion. As long as this is the case--because they do exist through some nature of their own--I could never eliminate them from their root." It is good though if I can eliminate this fear from my heart, and rely on the practice of making great efforts to remove my mental afflictions, through working to develop the wisdom which perceives emptiness. Given that I therefore have at the present moment the ability to remove these afflictions, it is not good on the other hand that I subject myself pointlessly to the sufferings of the lower realms, to hells and the rest. Why should I put myself through these pains? Some commentators have also explained the previous lines as referring to the fact that, once we remove the seeds for the mental afflictions, they can no longer stay in these various places. 10 Listening to the Doctor

wylie: gang la sbyin na slob ma la ni'o, ,slob ma ci 'dra ba zhig snyam na, khyad par gnyis dang ldan pa ste dang po ni, sangs rgyas dang chos dang dge 'dun te dkon mchog gsum la skyabs su song ba ste skyabs 'gro thun mong ma yin pa'i sdom pa dang ldan pa'o, ,gnyis pa ni, bsam pa dag pa ste smon pa dang 'jug pa'i byang chub kyi sems rnam pa gnyis tshul bzhin du bskyed pa'o, ,'dis ni sngags dang phar phyin gyi theg pa gnyis kyi thun mong ba'i lam gyi rim par la blo legs par sbyangs pa la gzhung 'di 'chang par bstan no
english: Who is it that we should grant this teaching on how to behave towards our Lama?  It should be granted to a worthy disciple.  And what is it that makes them worthy?  The disciple should be possessed of two characteristics. First of all, they must be someone who has already gone for shelter to the Three Jewels: to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Community.  That is to say, they must be possessed of the unique vow of refuge. The disciple must secondly be "one of a pure heart," which means that they must have given birth, in the proper way, to both forms of the Wish for enlightenment: the Wish as a prayer, and the Wish in action. The point here that the root text of the Fifty Verses is making is that a potential disciple for its teaching must be one whose mind has been perfectly prepared, by using the steps of the path which are shared by both the way of the secret word and the way of the perfections. ***

acip: DE LA YUL LNGA BSTEN PAS NYON MONGS SKYE LA, DE YANG NGAN 'GRO'I RGYUR 'GYUR ZHES BRTZAD PA LA, YUL BSTEN PA LAS SKYES PA'I NYON MONGS LA NYAN THOS LA SOGS PA DE KHO NA NYID MA RTOGS PA LA NGAN 'GRO'I RGYU DANG, RTOGS PA LA SANGS RGYAS KYI RGYUR 'GYUR BA GNYIS SU PHYE BA'I LAN MDZAD KYI, 'DOD YON BSTEN PA LAS NYON MONGS MI SKYED CES MA GSUNGS SO,,
wylie: de la yul lnga bsten pas nyon mongs skye la, de yang ngan 'gro'i rgyur 'gyur zhes brtsad pa la, yul bsten pa las skyes pa'i nyon mongs la nyan thos la sogs pa de kho na nyid ma rtogs pa la ngan 'gro'i rgyu dang, rtogs pa la sangs rgyas kyi rgyur 'gyur ba gnyis su phye ba'i lan mdzad kyi, 'dod yon bsten pa las nyon mongs mi skyed ces ma gsungs so
english: Someone might react to this by arguing that using the five objects of the senses leads to a mental affliction, and that this then acts as a cause that leads us to the births of misery.  The way you have to phrase the answer to this argument is by splitting your reply; you need to say, "When you do use these objects, it gives rise to mental afflictions.  For those like practitioners on the listener track who have yet to perceive suchness, these mental afflictions act as a cause for the lower births.  For those who have perceived suchness, these same afflictions act as a cause for enlightenment."  You shouldn't try to respond to this argument by saying that using these objects doesn't give rise to mental afflictions.
